definition: Successive parabolic interpolation is a technique for finding the extremum (minimum or maximum) of a continuous unimodal function by successively fitting parabolas (polynomials of degree two) to a function of one variable at three unique points or, in general, a function of n variables at 1+n(n+3)/2 points, and at each iteration replacing the "oldest" point with the extremum of the fitted parabola..
details: Successive parabolic interpolation is a technique for finding the extremum (minimum or maximum) of a continuous unimodal function by successively fitting parabolas (polynomials of degree two) to a function of one variable at three unique points or, in general, a function of n variables at 1+n(n+3)/2 points, and at each iteration replacing the "oldest" point with the extremum of the fitted parabola.

explainer.lead: An optimization routine that finds the optimum of a smooth one-variable function by repeatedly fitting parabolas through sampled points rather than using derivatives. It matters because it converges fast on well-behaved unimodal functions with cheap function evaluations.

tiers.eli5: Imagine guessing where a hill peaks by drawing a smooth curve through three spots on its slope, then checking the top of that curve and repeating with the newest three points.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it as a derivative-free line search inside larger optimizers, or for one-dimensional tuning when evaluations are expensive; the common pitfall is that it can diverge or converge to the wrong point if the function is not unimodal.
tiers.paperLevel: Fit a degree-two polynomial through three distinct points of a continuous unimodal function and replace the oldest point with the parabola's extremum each iteration; in n variables, 1+n(n+3)/2 points are used. It is not guaranteed to converge without safeguards.

explainer.example: For f(x)=(x-2)^2, fit a parabola through x=0,1,3, take its vertex as the new point, drop the oldest sample, and repeat until the estimate settles near x=2.
